title: Analytic properties of cross-click operators in passive multi-basis photodetection: monotonicity, exact convergence rates, and dimension reduction for quantum key distribution
abstract: Cross-click operators, the POVM elements for simultaneous clicks in detectors assigned to different measurement bases, are used in QKD and entanglement-verification analyses with realistic threshold detectors to bound multiphoton contributions. Earlier applications verified the needed growth of the minimum eigenvalue $f^{(n)}$ on the $n$-photon subspace only numerically over finite sectors. This work gives an analytic characterization for passive linear-optical analyzers with arbitrary efficiency mismatch and dark counts. The key observation is that every silence operator is the second quantization $Γ(A)$ of an explicit single-photon contraction $A$, whose $n$-photon restriction is $A^{\otimes n}$ on $\mathrm{Sym}^n$. This yields: (i) monotonicity $f^{(n+1)}\ge f^{(n)}$; (ii) two-sided exponential bounds $\max_b γ_b|A_b|^n \le 1-f^{(n)} \le \sum_b γ_b|A_b|^n$, which determine the exact asymptotic convergence rate from single-photon spectral data; (iii) for ideal detectors and $n\ge1$, the exact formula $f^{(n)}=1-\sum_b p_b^n$; and (iv) an exact factorization $1-f^{(n_A,n_B)}=(1-f_A^{(n_A)})(1-f_B^{(n_B)})$ for the two-party cross-click operator. The results apply to polarization, time-bin, and spatial-mode analyzers within the stated threshold-detector model. As an application, we obtain closed-form photon-number weight bounds used in detection-efficiency-mismatch analyses, replacing finite-sector Fock-space numerics by formulas valid for all photon numbers.
summary: This paper analytically characterizes cross-click operators used in analyzing photodetection processes for quantum key distribution. By showing these operators are related to symmetric tensor powers, the authors derive exact formulas for spectral properties like monotonicity and convergence rates. This breakthrough replaces complex Fock-space numerics with general, closed-form bounds essential for rigorous QKD security proofs.
main_problem: To provide a sharp analytic characterization of the spectral behavior of cross-click operators in passive multi-basis photodetection for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) security proofs.
main_result: The work establishes monotonicity, two-sided exponential bounds, and exact factorization formulas for these operators, replacing finite-sector numerical calculations with closed-form analytical results.
method: The analysis leverages the structural property that silence operators are second quantizations of explicit single-photon contractions, allowing properties to be derived from tensor algebra and operator inequalities.
model_or_system: The system models passive linear-optical analyzers using threshold single-photon detectors, applicable to polarization, time-bin, or spatial-mode qubits in QKD setups.
key_observables: The minimum eigenvalue of the cross-click operator on the n-photon subspace, $f^{(n)}$, and related quantities like $1 - f(n)$ for the no-cross-click operator.
important_parameters: Detector efficiencies ($\eta_d$), dark-count probabilities ($\epsilon_d$), and the photon number ($n$).
main_assumptions: The results hold for arbitrary passive analyzers with specified parameters, assuming independent dark counts and uncorrelated efficiencies; afterpulsing breaks the product structure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate a running example (six-state polarization analyzer) showing cross-click probability $f(n)$ versus photon number, tracking the closed-form convergence rate $\max_b \|A_b\|$, and visualizing joint operator factorization $f(n_A, n_B)$.
paper_structure: The paper develops its findings by first establishing the structural lemma for silence operators, then proving monotonicity (Theorem 1), deriving two-sided exponential bounds (Theorem 2) to find the exact convergence rate, and finally presenting special cases like ideal detectors and joint operator factorization.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous analytical tools to quantify security loopholes in QKD protocols caused by detector imperfections, moving beyond computationally intensive numerical simulations into closed-form physics.
